Summary:
  Quick Optimize walkthrough focusing on batching and prefix / KV cache recommendations for CrestPay's chat summarization use case. Covered cost model assumptions, hit rate sensitivity, memory/latency tradeoffs, and next steps to run benchmarks on Dedicated.

Topics:
  - Current infra and tokens per request
  - Batching: target batch sizes, latency windows, tail latency
  - KV cache: prefix vs full-response cache, eviction, memory sizing
  - Cost model: token cost assumptions, impact of cache hit rate and batching on TCO
  - Security considerations (KMS, data residency)

Action items (recorded verbally in call):
  - Samir to share benchmark scripts and playbook
  - CrestPay to share seq length distribution and QPS targets
  - Jordan to send pricing and SOC2/KMS notes

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: all right folks thanks for taking the time, um this is Jordan from Redwood, with Samir our solutions engineer. today we wanted to walk through Optimize — specifically batching and the KV / prefix cache recommendations that we think will help CrestPay reduce per-token cost while keeping latency tight.
[00:18] Elena Morris: yeah thanks, we're excited, been looking forward to the cost modeling, we get a lot of chats per minute and the cost is starting to stack up so curious about cache options.
[00:27] Samir Patel: cool, quick agenda — 1) understand your current request mix, 2) show recommended batching policy and expected latency impact, 3) show prefix / KV cache approach and run through a simple cost model. sound ok?
[00:39] David Kim: yep, that works. for context our infra is k8s on GCP, we run a mix of hosted endpoints and a few internal endpoints, and we do plan to test dedicated infra for production.
[00:51] Ravi Shah: product goals: sub-300ms median latency on quick lookups, and keeping token spend under our 3% of revenue cap.
[01:02] Samir Patel: great. Elena, do you have approximate request distribution? sequence lengths?
[01:07] Elena Morris: yeah rough numbers: 65% of requests are short 40-120 tokens (quick Q/A), 25% mid 200-600 tokens (summaries), 10% long 1k+ (full transcript condense). Peak qps about 120 rps across region.
[01:24] Jordan Lee: perfect that's helpful. two levers we usually recommend: batching at the runtime layer to increase throughput and reduce per-token overhead, and KV/prefix caching for predictable repeated prefixes like system prompts or chat history.
[01:38] Samir Patel: quick note on batching: batching gives you GPU utilization gains but for short-sequence low-latency traffic you need to pick batching windows carefully so tail latency stays acceptable. we often use a 20-50ms latency window with dynamic batch size that caps at the device's optimal batch. in our cost model we simulate batching by assuming X ms window and arrival rate.
[02:01] David Kim: ok, can you quantify expected latency add if we set 25ms window and typical 120 rps?
[02:07] Samir Patel: rough math — at 120 rps that's 8.3ms inter-arrival avg; with a 25ms window you'll typically collect ~3 requests per batch average, so batching overhead is about the window (25ms) plus kernel execution. median may rise by ~15-30ms but p95 depends on kernel saturation. if you want sub-300ms median we're comfortable.
[02:28] Elena Morris: that sounds fine for most flows. for the short Q/A we might want lower window. can we do per-route policies?
[02:34] Jordan Lee: yes per-route latency SLOs and batching policies in the Console — you can set lower windows for the quick routes and more aggressive batching for summary routes.
[02:41] Ravi Shah: talk to me about KV cache — what's the difference between prefix cache and full KV cache?
[02:46] Samir Patel: good question. prefix cache stores only the KV states for common prefixes (e.g., system prompt + recent messages) so for follow-on tokens you get cache hits that skip re-computation of the attention up to the prefix length. full-response cache stores full completed outputs for identical requests (great for deterministic queries). prefix is super useful for chat where much of the context repeats.
[03:06] Samir Patel: in practice, we see prefix cache hit rates of 20-50% in chat flows with stable system prompts and repeated instruction patterns; your mix will determine savings.
[03:14] Elena Morris: what about memory sizing? we have constraints on GPU memory and also on our dedicated nodes budget.
[03:20] Samir Patel: prefix cache is KV cache stored either on the serving node memory or an external KV (Redis/rocks) depending on scale. memory per cached prefix is roughly model-dependent: for a 16k-dim KV store and 1k-token prefix it's on the order of tens to low hundreds of megabytes per model shard — our tooling estimates required cache memory given hit rate targets. for Dedicated we can allocate larger KV regions; for Hosted we use cross-request KV with eviction.
[03:44] David Kim: we can't allocate big persistent memory on our short-term nodes, we'd need to use external redis. latency penalty?
[03:49] Samir Patel: external redis adds network hop; we typically see 1-5ms extra per lookup inside the batch window. but if hit rate is high, net win is big because you avoid model forward passes that cost tens to hundreds of ms depending on model size.
[04:03] Jordan Lee: jumping to cost model — baseline assumptions we used in the deck: model token compute cost equivalent to $X per 1M tokens (we used a placeholder $8/M for the larger gpt-style open model), and a cached token is effectively near zero CPU cost aside from lookup overhead; batching reduces per-token compute by ~20-40% depending on seq length distribution.
[04:25] Ravi Shah: can you show an example calc for our mix?
[04:28] Samir Patel: sure, simple example: assume 1M short requests at avg 80 tokens => 80M tokens. at $8/M that's $640. if we get a 30% prefix hit rate that avoids 30% of those tokens served => saves ~$192. add batching gains — if batching reduces effective compute by 25% across mid/long requests you compound savings. so combined we estimate 35-45% reduction in token bill for chat-heavy apps in our sim.
[04:55] Elena Morris: nice. what's sensitivity to hit rate? if only 10% hit rate then savings are small, right?
[05:01] Samir Patel: correct. that sensitivity table is in the spreadsheet I'll share — moving from 10% to 40% hit rate is non-linear because cached prefixes also change effective batching (cache hits reduce compute time and free GPU to accept more batches).
[05:15] David Kim: curious about consistency / staleness if we cache prefixes that include recent user messages — how do you ensure correctness?
[05:21] Samir Patel: prefix caches are keyed on canonicalized conversation state; if you have per-user ephemeral context we recommend a short time-to-live or deterministic invalidation on write (e.g., any new user message invalidates later prefixes). also you can scope caches to system prompt + last N stable messages to avoid stale personalization.
[05:41] Ravi Shah: security questions — for KV that contains potentially PII, do you encrypt at rest and with KMS?
[05:47] Jordan Lee: yes, for Private and Dedicated we offer KMS integrations and customer-managed keys; even for Hosted we encrypt at rest and you can opt into our enterprise KMS handling for dedicated contracts. we'll include the SOC2 highlights and KMS notes in the follow-up.
[06:02] Elena Morris: good. about benchmarking — what does Redwood need from us to run a representative run?
[06:06] Samir Patel: ideally: 1) sequence length histogram, 2) QPS targets and concurrency pattern (burstiness), 3) sample prompt templates, and 4) security requirements (whether can share sample payloads). with those we can simulate traffic and run a 1-2 hour benchmark on Dedicated or Hosted with KV enabled.
[06:22] Elena Morris: we can anonymize payloads and provide histograms.
[06:25] Jordan Lee: perfect.
[06:27] Samir Patel: couple more nitty gritty — batching interplay with KV: when you have a high rate of cache hits you actually get smaller compute batches because requests short-circuit; we model that by splitting traffic into "hit" and "miss" groups and estimating device utilization. also for sequences that grow during generation (streaming), we keep KV warm so subsequent calls benefit.
[06:51] David Kim: streaming — any impact on p95? we stream partial tokens to clients frequently.
[06:56] Samir Patel: streaming interacts with batching windows; we send the first token as soon as decode starts but we batch the initial forward; there's a tradeoff between initial token latency and throughput, but we've optimized our runtime to provide partial tokens quickly while still benefiting from batching for the heavy compute parts.
[07:12] Ravi Shah: deployment modes — if we go Dedicated, can we reserve memory for KV in node spec?
[07:18] Jordan Lee: yes, Dedicated nodes can be right-sized and we can reserve large cache memory. for on-prem or VPC deployments we support mounting a customer-managed Redis or using our in-memory option.
[07:27] Elena Morris: ok can you run through a sample cost table row-by-row? maybe with our numbers?
[07:33] Samir Patel: sure — I'll read out a compact row, details will be in the sheet: baseline tokens per month: 80M tokens short, 50M tokens mid, 10M tokens long => total 140M. baseline cost at $8/M => $1120. with prefix cache at 30% hit on short and 15% on mid, plus batching saving 20% on mid/long, net compute tokens equivalent drops to ~78M effective tokens => ~$624, so rough saving ~44%.
[08:02] Ravi Shah: good. does this include infra (VM/GPU) amortization for Dedicated?
[08:06] Samir Patel: that was pure token compute cost. we can fold in Dedicated hourly amortization (e.g., reserved instances) and show break-even horizon. in many cases if you have sustained throughput > X you get dedicated infra cheaper by Y% vs hosted. the spreadsheet has a break-even calc.
[08:23] Elena Morris: interested in that break-even; we have predictable sustained throughput.
[08:26] Jordan Lee: we'll include a comparison: hosted per-token vs dedicated amortized cost with reserved commit levels.
[08:31] David Kim: another operational question — eviction policy and cold start after deploys?
[08:36] Samir Patel: we use LRU by default for our in-memory KV; for Redis-backed caches you can pick TTLs. during deploys we pre-warm common prefixes by replaying a sample of recent traffic so cold penalty is minimized.
[08:50] Ravi Shah: what's the expected latency penalty for cold miss?
[08:53] Samir Patel: cold miss is same as normal miss — full forward pass. depending on model that could be 50-200ms for mid-sized models. warm hit will cut that dramatically.
[08:59] Elena Morris: ok. any limitations on tokenization or model support? like quantized models or attention types?
[09:04] Samir Patel: prefix KV works for decoder-style transformer models we support. we also have quantization-friendly runtimes; some very aggressive quantization reduces memory cost but may impact latency/throughput slightly. we'll flag model compatibility in the model catalog and recommendations.
[09:18] Jordan Lee: high-level recap: 1) send us sequences and QPS, 2) we'll simulate and share a tailored spreadsheet with sensitivity, 3) run a 2h benchmark on Dedicated with KV config, 4) follow up with pricing + security docs.
[09:33] Elena Morris: sounds good, we'll get histograms to you by Monday.
[09:36] David Kim: any blockers from infra side for benchmarking?
[09:39] Samir Patel: just network access if we provision a dedicated test cluster in your VPC; otherwise we can run in our dedicated pool and mirror traffic.
[09:47] Ravi Shah: ok let's target next Wed for the benchmark. Samir can you send available time slots?
[09:51] Samir Patel: will do — I'll send a Doodle and the playbook.
[09:54] Jordan Lee: thanks everyone, we'll send the spreadsheet and docs right after.
[09:58] Elena Morris: thank you.

[END]
